mcqs.question: Why does DDD recommend that a single database transaction should touch at most one aggregate?
options: Databases enforce a hard limit of one write per transaction
It makes queries run faster by reducing the number of joined tables
It lets consistency be reasoned about locally, one aggregate at a time, instead of needing atomic guarantees across the whole object graph
It's required by most ORMs' transaction APIs
mcqs.explanation: Scoping transactions to one aggregate is a deliberate design constraint that keeps consistency reasoning local and avoids distributed-transaction complexity — it's not a database limitation, an ORM requirement, or primarily a performance trick for joins.

mcqs.question: In the Order aggregate, why should outside code call order.addLineItem() instead of constructing an OrderLineItem directly and appending it?
options: The aggregate root is the only object outside code may reference, so it's the only path that can enforce the aggregate's invariants
Constructing objects directly is slower than calling a method
OrderLineItem doesn't have a public constructor in most languages
It matches naming conventions more than it affects correctness
mcqs.explanation: The aggregate root is deliberately the sole entry point so that every change is routed through code that can check invariants (like recomputing totals); bypassing it by constructing internals directly defeats the entire purpose of the boundary. This is a correctness mechanism, not a naming or performance convention.

mcqs.question: A team is considering adding an OrderLineItemRepository alongside their existing OrderRepository. What does this suggest?
options: This is a normal and expected pattern in DDD once an aggregate has more than one entity
It will improve performance by allowing line items to be queried independently
It's likely a sign the aggregate boundary is drawn wrong, since a non-root entity shouldn't be loaded or saved independently
It's required whenever an entity has its own database table
mcqs.explanation: The rule is one repository per aggregate root — OrderLineItem should never be loaded or persisted independently of the Order it belongs to, so wanting a separate repository for it usually signals the aggregate boundary needs rethinking, not a performance opportunity to pursue.

mcqs.question: A transfer between two Account aggregates needs insufficient-funds checks and currency matching. Where should this logic live?
options: In a domain service, since it's a business concept that doesn't naturally belong to either Account alone
As a method on the source Account, which reaches into the destination Account directly
In the application/use-case layer, since it coordinates two objects
Duplicated as a method on both Account entities
mcqs.explanation: A domain service is exactly the pattern for logic that coordinates across aggregates without belonging to either one — putting it on one Account would violate the rule that an aggregate is only modified through its own root, and it's genuine domain logic, not application-workflow orchestration.

mcqs.question: Why are domain events named in the past tense (OrderPlaced, not PlaceOrder)?
options: Past tense is a stylistic convention with no functional meaning
It's required by most message queue libraries
A domain event records a fact that already happened, decoupling the aggregate from whatever reacts to that fact later
It distinguishes events from aggregate constructors
mcqs.explanation: Naming reflects the semantics: an event is a record of something that has already occurred, raised by the aggregate as a side effect, with listeners reacting independently — the aggregate itself never knows or cares who's listening, which is the actual point of the decoupling.

mcqs.question: A team models an entire Warehouse with all its InventoryItems as one aggregate. Under concurrent load, what problem does this cause?
options: The aggregate will exceed most databases' maximum row size
Repositories will need to be duplicated for each inventory item
Domain events can no longer be raised from within the aggregate
Unrelated writes to different inventory items get serialized behind the same lock, capping the whole warehouse's write throughput
mcqs.explanation: An aggregate this large forces every operation — even ones touching completely unrelated items — through the same root and the same transactional lock, creating contention with no real business justification. Row size, repository duplication, and event-raising aren't the actual failure mode here.
